title: Saturn’s moon Enceladus sprays its ocean into space and feeds one of Saturn’s rings

cover.alt: Backlit jets of ice and vapour spraying from the south pole of Saturn’s moon Enceladus, a thin bright crescent against black space.

body: Enceladus is only about 500 km across, yet in 2005 the Cassini spacecraft found jets near its south pole blasting water vapour and ice grains into space, about **200 kg every second** from more than 100 geysers. The spray comes from a salty ocean 26 to 31 km deep under an ice shell 30 to 40 km thick, kept warm by tides: an orbital resonance with the moon Dione keeps Enceladus’s orbit slightly eccentric, and Saturn’s pull flexes and heats it. Some of the vapour falls back as snow, now several hundred metres thick, which makes Enceladus the most reflective body in the Solar System; the rest escapes and supplies most of Saturn’s E ring. In 2015 Cassini flew through a plume just 48 km above the surface and found hydrogen, salts, silica grains and organic molecules.

slides.question: How much material do the geysers throw out every second?
slides.explanation: About 200 kg a second (one estimate of the water vapour alone is 250 kg/s). That adds up to roughly 17,000 tonnes a day.

slides.label: geysers found along the four ‘tiger stripes’ near the south pole
slides.text: The stripes are long fractures bounded by ridges, where ocean water escapes through the ice.

steps.label: Saturn’s tides heat and crack the ice shell
Ocean water rises through the fissures
Geysers spray vapour and ice grains
Some falls back as bright snow
The rest feeds Saturn’s E ring

slides.heading: Cold outside, liquid inside
slides.note: The mean noon surface temperature is −198 °C, yet 30 to 40 km down there is liquid water

slides.alt: A thin bright crescent of Enceladus with a faint plume rising from its edge, photographed by Cassini during a flyby.
slides.caption: The Cassini spacecraft’s unprocessed view of the plume during its October 2015 flight through it, taken from about 190,000 km.

slides.heading: What Cassini tasted in the spray
items: Water vapour, about 91% of the gas
Silica grains, a hint of hot rock

slides.question: Why is Enceladus the most reflective body in the Solar System?
options: Fresh snow from the plumes coats it
It is made of polished metal
It has no craters at all
slides.explanation: Plume material falls back as fresh, clean ice and snow, several hundred metres thick in places, so the surface reflects most of the sunlight that hits it.
